Photo geotagging without a track file

No GPX? Use nearby iPhone photos as location clues.

iPhone photos from the same outing can place camera photos between known times and locations. Every result stays a reviewable suggestion—not recovered GPS.

Published and reviewed September 17, 2026

How the no-GPX method works

Build a location timeline from photos you already took.

  1. LensPin finds eligible iPhone anchorsOnly geotagged photos that can be identified as Apple iPhone photos become location evidence. Downloaded images and unknown sources are excluded.
  2. It compares the nearest timesFor each camera photo, LensPin searches for an eligible iPhone photo before and after the adjusted capture time.
  3. It checks both time and distanceTwo anchors in the same small area support one another. Widely separated anchors indicate movement and require more caution.
  4. You review the suggested pointSee both anchor thumbnails, their time differences, the map, and the reason behind the status before selecting anything.

What makes evidence stronger

Close in time, close in place, visible on both sides.

2

Before and after

An iPhone photo on each side of the camera capture usually explains the interval better than a single anchor.

↔

Locations agree

If the anchors sit within the same small area, LensPin has evidence that you stayed nearby between those times.

5m

Short time gaps

A five-minute gap is easier to trust than a gap of an hour. Your chosen maximum anchor interval is a hard eligibility limit.

When the timeline shows movement

LensPin does not draw a straight line between distant photos.

If the two iPhone anchors are more than 300 metres apart, LensPin uses the nearer-in-time anchor rather than pretending the exact route between them is known. The confidence is reduced so you review the suggestion.

Nearby anchors

Same-area evidence

  • Use the shared area as the suggestion
  • Give more weight when both times are close
  • Explain how the anchors support the result
Distant anchors

Movement evidence

  • Do not invent a travel path
  • Favor the nearer time with lower confidence
  • Give no suggestion when even that anchor is too far away in time

Only one nearby iPhone photo?

A one-sided clue can help, but it needs more caution.

LensPin can form a suggestion from one eligible anchor when it is close enough in time. Because there is no second photo to show whether you stayed in the same area, the result receives a penalty and may land in Review.

Example:

A geotagged iPhone photo at 10:02 may be useful for a camera photo at 10:07. The same anchor is much less informative for a camera photo at 11:30.

Designed around your library

Local matching, with narrow source eligibility.

Photos stay on the device

LensPin reads Photos metadata and creates suggestions locally. Your images are not uploaded for matching.

Unknown images are not anchors

A geotagged image from the web should not move your camera photos. LensPin only uses location photos it can identify as iPhone photos.

Existing locations are excluded

Candidate camera photos must have no location. LensPin rechecks before adding one.

Time-zone lookup is disclosed

Automatic local-time display may send a small number of coordinates to Apple's geocoding service; it never sends the photos themselves.

Know the limits

This method needs photos from the same outing.

No iPhone photos nearby in time

There may be no responsible location suggestion. LensPin reports the nearest available gaps instead of silently widening the window.

Camera clock offset

A wrong camera time affects anchor selection. Calibrate with a known moment before reviewing a large batch.

Fast movement

Driving, trains, and flights can cover large distances between photos. A GPX track usually gives denser evidence for these trips.

Approximate inference

The result indicates a place supported by the timeline. It is not the exact location the camera failed to record.

Have a track after all?

GPX gives LensPin a denser timeline.

Use the track as primary evidence and nearby iPhone photos as a cross-check.
